title: Structural biochemistry
description: Le domande dei Test A e B dell'anno scorso, più domande nuove sugli stessi argomenti. Ogni risposta ha la sua spiegazione.
description_en: Last year's Test A and B questions, plus new questions on the same topics. Every answer comes with an explanation.

A.question: Which four elements account for about 96% of the human body’s mass?
A.explanation: Oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen make up about 96% of body mass; the others are present in much smaller amounts.

A.question: The number of protons in an atom determines:
A.explanation: The atomic number (number of protons) defines which element an atom is; neutrons change the isotope, not the element.

A.question: The quantum number n defines:
A.explanation: n is the principal quantum number: it sets the energy level (shell) of the orbital. Shape is l, orientation is ml, spin is ms.

A.question: Which rule states that two electrons cannot have the same set of four quantum numbers?
A.explanation: Pauli exclusion principle: no two electrons share all four quantum numbers, so an orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins.

A.question: Electronegativity represents:
options: The energy needed to remove an electron
The tendency of an atom to attract electrons in a bond
A.explanation: Electronegativity is the tendency to attract shared electrons in a bond. The energy needed to remove an electron is the ionization energy.

A.question: Carbon’s ability to form four covalent bonds is due to:
A.explanation: In sp³ hybridization the 2s and three 2p orbitals mix into four equivalent orbitals, one for each covalent bond.

A.question: The ability of carbon to form long chains and complex branched molecules is mainly due to:
A.explanation: With four bonds available (tetravalence), carbon can bind other carbons in chains, branches and rings.

A.question: Two molecules that are mirror, non-superimposable images are:
A.explanation: Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images, like left and right hands. Epimers and diastereomers are not mirror images.

A.question: The α and β forms of glucose differ in:
options: Orientation of the hydroxyl on the anomeric carbon
A.explanation: α and β anomers differ only in the position of the OH on the anomeric carbon (C1 in glucose): down for α, up for β in the Haworth projection.

A.question: A pyranose ring in carbohydrates contains:
A.explanation: Pyranose = 6-membered ring like pyran: 5 carbons and 1 oxygen. A furanose ring has 5 atoms (4 C + 1 O).

A.question: The main energy-storage polysaccharide in animals is:
A.explanation: Animals store glucose as glycogen, mainly in liver and muscle. Starch (amylose, amylopectin) is the plant equivalent.

A.question: Cellulose differs from starch because:
options: It is made of fructose units
A.explanation: Cellulose uses β(1→4) links that keep the chain straight; starch uses α(1→4) links that make it bend into a helix.

A.question: Lipids are generally characterized by:
A.explanation: Lipids are defined by their insolubility in water, not by a common structure.

A.question: Saturated fatty acids have:
A.explanation: Saturated means no C=C double bonds: the chain carries the maximum number of hydrogens.

A.question: The ω-3 and ω-6 fatty acids differ in:
options: Position of the first double bond from the methyl end
A.explanation: ω-3 and ω-6 indicate where the first double bond is, counting from the methyl (ω) end of the chain.

A.question: Phospholipids are amphipathic molecules because they contain:
options: A polar head and nonpolar tails
A.explanation: A phospholipid has a polar (hydrophilic) head and nonpolar (hydrophobic) tails: this is what makes it amphipathic and lets it form bilayers.

A.question: In sphingolipids, the backbone is:
A.explanation: Sphingolipids are built on sphingosine, an amino alcohol, instead of glycerol.

A.question: Cholesterol is essential for membranes because it:
A.explanation: Cholesterol slots between phospholipids, making the bilayer less fluid, more stable and a better barrier.

A.question: Amino acids in proteins are:
A.explanation: Proteins are built from L-amino acids; sugars in nature are mostly D.

A.question: The peptide bond is:
options: A partial double bond that restricts rotation
A.explanation: The peptide bond has partial double-bond character (resonance), so it is planar and does not rotate freely.

A.question: The α-helix is stabilized mainly by:
A.explanation: In the α-helix, the C=O of residue n bonds to the N–H of residue n+4: hydrogen bonds within the backbone.

A.question: In β-sheets, peptide chains are stabilized by:
A.explanation: β-sheets are held by hydrogen bonds between the backbone C=O and N–H of neighbouring strands, not by the side chains.

A.question: The Ramachandran plot shows:
options: Allowed φ and ψ angles in a polypeptide
A.explanation: The Ramachandran plot shows which φ and ψ backbone angles are allowed, and so which secondary structures are possible.

A.question: The quaternary structure of a protein refers to:
options: The folding of a single chain
A.explanation: Quaternary structure is how several polypeptide chains (subunits) assemble, as in hemoglobin's four chains.

A.question: Collagen is composed of:
A.explanation: Each collagen chain is a left-handed helix (not an α-helix); three chains wind together in a right-handed triple helix.

A.question: The repeating amino acid motif in collagen is:
A.explanation: Gly-X-Y: glycine every third residue fits in the crowded centre of the triple helix; X and Y are often Pro and hydroxyproline.

A.question: Myoglobin’s main role is to:
A.explanation: Myoglobin is in muscle and stores O₂; its high affinity lets it hold oxygen until the muscle needs it.

A.question: Hemoglobin’s sigmoidal oxygen-binding curve reflects:
A.explanation: A sigmoidal curve means cooperativity: once one subunit binds O₂, the others bind it more easily (T to R transition).

A.question: The Bohr effect describes:
options: Increased O₂ affinity at low pH
Decreased O₂ affinity at low pH
The binding of CO to hemoglobin
The oxidation of Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺
A.explanation: Bohr effect: lower pH (more H⁺ and CO₂, as in working muscle) lowers hemoglobin's O₂ affinity, so more O₂ is released.

A.question: Enzymes accelerate reactions by:
A.explanation: Enzymes lower the activation energy by stabilizing the transition state; they do not change the equilibrium.

A.question: Phosphorylation as a post-translational modification typically occurs on:
A.explanation: Only serine, threonine and tyrosine have the OH group on their side chain that kinases phosphorylate.

B.question: Which subatomic particle carries a positive charge?
B.explanation: Protons are positive, electrons negative, neutrons neutral.

B.question: The atomic number of an element corresponds to:
options: The number of electrons in a neutral atom
The sum of neutrons and protons
B.explanation: The atomic number is the number of protons, which in a neutral atom equals the number of electrons.

B.question: Which orbital can hold a maximum of 10 electrons?
B.explanation: d sublevels have 5 orbitals × 2 electrons = 10. s holds 2, p 6, f 14.

B.question: The tendency of an atom to attract shared electrons is called:
B.explanation: That is electronegativity. Ionization energy is the energy to remove an electron; electron affinity is the energy change when one is gained.

B.question: Which statement about noble gases is correct?
options: They have complete outer electron shells and are chemically inert
They are the most reactive nonmetals.
B.explanation: Noble gases have a full outer shell, so they are very stable and hardly react (only Kr and Xe react, with F and O).

B.question: Which property of carbon allows it to create the complex molecules essential for life?
options: It can form four stable covalent bonds in multiple arrangements
B.explanation: Four stable covalent bonds in many arrangements (chains, branches, rings, double bonds) give carbon its variety.

B.question: The geometry of methane (CH₄) is:
B.explanation: Methane is sp³: four bonds pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron, at about 109.5°.

B.question: Molecules with the same formula but different spatial arrangements around a double bond are:
B.explanation: Different arrangements around a double bond (cis/trans or E/Z) are geometric isomers: the double bond does not rotate.

B.question: A sugar containing six carbon atoms is called a:
B.explanation: Hexose = 6 carbons (glucose, fructose, galactose). Pentoses have 5, trioses 3.

B.question: The bond linking monosaccharides in disaccharides and polysaccharides is called a:
B.explanation: Monosaccharides are linked by glycosidic bonds; peptide bonds link amino acids, ester bonds are typical of lipids.

B.question: The polysaccharide that forms plant cell walls is:
B.explanation: Cellulose, with β(1→4) links, forms the plant cell wall. Glycogen is the animal storage form.

B.question: The main function of carbohydrates in living organisms is to:
options: Serve as a primary source of energy
B.explanation: Carbohydrates are the main source of energy; DNA carries genetic information and lipids form membranes.

B.question: Which of the following is not a lipid?
B.explanation: Glycogen is a polysaccharide (a carbohydrate), not a lipid.

B.question: Which type of fatty acid is liquid at room temperature?
B.explanation: Double bonds put kinks in the chain, so unsaturated fatty acids pack loosely and stay liquid (oils).

B.question: The head group of a phospholipid is typically:
B.explanation: Phospholipid heads are polar and hydrophilic, facing the water on both sides of the bilayer.

B.question: Which lipid component predominates in the myelin sheath?
B.explanation: Sphingomyelin is especially concentrated in the myelin sheath around nerve axons.

B.question: The major structural difference between sphingolipids and phosphoglycerides is:
options: Sphingolipids contain sphingosine instead of glycerol
B.explanation: Sphingolipids have sphingosine as backbone instead of glycerol; both can carry phosphate.

B.question: Which molecule serves as the precursor of all steroids?
B.explanation: Squalene, a triterpene built from isoprene units, is the precursor of cholesterol and therefore of steroids.

B.question: Which functional group is present in all amino acids?
B.explanation: Every amino acid has an amino group and a carboxyl group on the α carbon; they differ in the side chain.

B.question: Peptide bonds form between:
options: An amino and a carboxyl group
B.explanation: A peptide bond joins the carboxyl group of one amino acid to the amino group of the next, releasing water.

B.question: The β-sheet is stabilized by:
B.explanation: β-sheets are held by hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms of adjacent strands.

B.question: Which level of protein structure consists of simple, repetitive folding patterns such as α-helices and β- sheets?
B.explanation: Secondary structure means local repeating patterns of the backbone: α-helices and β-sheets.

B.question: A disulfide bond forms between two residues of:
B.explanation: Only cysteine has a thiol (–SH) group; two of them oxidize into a disulfide bridge.

B.question: Which type of interaction mainly drives nonpolar amino acid side chains to the interior of a folded protein?
B.explanation: Hydrophobic interactions: nonpolar side chains gather inside, away from water.

B.question: The basic structural unit of collagen is made of:
B.explanation: Tropocollagen, the basic unit, is three left-handed helices wound into a right-handed superhelix.

B.question: Collagen structure and stability depend largely on the presence of:
B.explanation: Glycine fits in the centre of the helix; proline and hydroxyproline are rigid and stabilize it.

B.question: The prosthetic group of hemoglobin responsible for oxygen binding is:
B.explanation: Heme (protoporphyrin IX with Fe²⁺) binds O₂. NADH, FAD and biotin are coenzymes of other enzymes.

B.question: The oxygen dissociation curve of myoglobin is:
B.explanation: One chain, one binding site, no cooperativity: myoglobin's curve is hyperbolic.

B.question: The cooperative binding of oxygen in hemoglobin is explained by:
B.explanation: Cooperativity comes from the T (low affinity) to R (high affinity) transition as O₂ binds. The Bohr effect is a regulation by pH.

B.question: Enzyme activity is generally lost at high temperature because:
B.explanation: Heat breaks the weak interactions holding the 3D structure: the enzyme denatures and the active site is lost.

B.question: An enzyme that moves a phosphate group from ATP to another molecule belongs to which class?
B.explanation: Moving a group (here phosphate) from one molecule to another is the job of transferases; kinases are transferases.

N.question: Which quantum number defines the shape of an orbital?
N.explanation: The secondary (azimuthal) quantum number l sets the sublevel and the shape: l = 0 is s (sphere), l = 1 is p (two lobes).

N.question: Hund's rule states that electrons in orbitals of the same sublevel:
options: Pair up as soon as possible
Occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins before pairing
N.explanation: Rule of maximum multiplicity: one electron per orbital, same spin, before any pairing. Carbon's two 2p electrons sit in separate orbitals.

N.question: The Aufbau principle states that electrons:
options: Cannot share all four quantum numbers
Fill orbitals in order of increasing energy
N.explanation: Aufbau means 'building up': lower-energy orbitals fill first. The other options describe Pauli and Hund.

N.question: How does ionization energy relate to atomic radius across the periodic table?
options: Both always increase down a group
N.explanation: Smaller atoms hold their electrons more tightly, so ionization energy rises where the radius shrinks: opposite trends.

N.question: How many electrons can a p sublevel hold?
N.explanation: A p sublevel has three orbitals (mₗ = −1, 0, +1), each with two electrons: 6.

N.question: Which two quantities are combined in Mulliken's electronegativity?
N.explanation: Mulliken: χ = ½(Ei − Eae). Electronegativity depends both on how hard it is to remove an electron and how much energy is gained by adding one.

N.question: The carbon atoms in ethylene (CH₂=CH₂) are hybridized:
N.explanation: A double bond means sp²: three hybrid orbitals (planar, 120°) plus one p orbital that forms the π bond.

N.question: Acetylene (CH≡CH) has carbons with which hybridization and geometry?
N.explanation: A triple bond means sp hybridization: two hybrid orbitals at 180°, so the molecule is linear.

N.question: Epimers are stereoisomers that:
options: Are mirror images of each other
Differ only around a double bond
Interconvert by rotating a single bond
Differ in configuration at only one chiral center
N.explanation: Epimers differ at exactly one chiral center (e.g. glucose and galactose at C4) and are not mirror images.

N.question: Anomers are:
options: Epimers at the anomeric (hemiacetal) carbon of a cyclic sugar
N.explanation: When the sugar closes into a ring, C1 becomes a new chiral center; the α and β forms are anomers.

N.question: Conformational isomers differ from configurational isomers because they:
options: Need bonds to break to interconvert
Interconvert by rotation around single bonds
N.explanation: Conformers (like the chair and boat forms) change into each other just by rotation; configurational isomers need bonds broken.

N.question: A chiral (stereogenic) carbon is a carbon:
N.explanation: Four different groups around the carbon make two non-superimposable mirror arrangements possible.

N.question: Naturally occurring sugars are mostly:
N.explanation: Sugars in nature are mostly D (OH of the last chiral carbon on the right in Fischer); amino acids are mostly L.

N.question: Fructose is classified as a:
N.explanation: Fructose has 6 carbons and a ketone group (C2): a ketohexose. Glucose is an aldohexose.

N.question: A furanose ring contains:
N.explanation: Furanose, like furan, is a 5-membered ring with one oxygen (fructose often takes this form). Pyranose is 6-membered.

N.question: Branch points in amylopectin and glycogen are formed by:
N.explanation: The main chain uses α(1→4) links; each branch starts with an α(1→6) link.

N.question: Compared with amylopectin, glycogen has:
N.explanation: Glycogen branches every 4–10 residues (amylopectin every 15–30): more chain ends, so glucose can be released faster.

N.question: Liver glycogen mainly serves to:
options: Keep blood glucose available between meals and during fasting
N.explanation: Liver glycogen releases glucose into the blood when food is not available, and runs out in 12–24 hours. Muscle glycogen fuels the muscle itself.

N.question: In the Haworth projection of α-D-glucopyranose, the OH on the anomeric carbon is:
options: In the plane of the ring
N.explanation: α: anomeric OH down (opposite to C6), β: up. In the Fischer–Tollens projection α is on the right.

N.question: Which change makes a fatty acid more fluid (lower melting point)?
N.explanation: More double bonds (kinks) and shorter chains reduce packing between chains: more fluid.

N.question: A triglyceride is:
options: Glycerol esterified with three fatty acids
Three glycerols linked to a phosphate
N.explanation: Triacylglycerol: glycerol's three OH groups each form an ester with a fatty acid. It is the main energy store.

N.question: Plasmalogens differ from phosphatidates because:
options: The chain at position 1 is linked by an ether bond
N.explanation: The ether bond at position 1 makes plasmalogens more stable, antioxidant and resistant to phospholipases.

N.question: During apoptosis, phosphatidylserine:
options: Moves to the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane
N.explanation: Normally PS sits in the inner leaflet; exposing it on the outside is an 'eat me' signal of a dying cell.

N.question: Gangliosides are acidic glycosphingolipids because they contain:
options: One or more sialic acid (NANA) residues
N.explanation: Sialic acid (N-acetylneuraminic acid) carries a negative charge. Cerebrosides and globosides have no NANA and are neutral.

N.question: A cerebroside is made of:
N.explanation: Cerebroside = ceramide + a single sugar (galactose or glucose). With phosphocholine it would be sphingomyelin.

N.question: Ceramide is formed by:
options: Sphingosine + a fatty acid linked by an amide bond
Two fatty acids linked by an ester bond
N.explanation: Ceramide is the core of all sphingolipids: sphingosine with a fatty acid attached through an amide bond.

N.question: The main role of brown adipose tissue is:
N.explanation: Brown fat cells are full of mitochondria (hence the colour) and burn lipids to produce heat. White fat stores energy.

N.question: How does cholesterol travel in the blood?
options: Bound to lipoproteins, mostly as cholesterol esters
N.explanation: Cholesterol is almost insoluble in water, so it travels in lipoproteins; about 65% is esterified.

N.question: Where are sphingolipids mainly found in the plasma membrane?
N.explanation: The membrane is asymmetric: sphingolipids and plasmalogens face outside, PS and PI face inside.

N.question: Steroids such as cholesterol are built from:
N.explanation: Terpenes are polymers of isoprene; squalene (a triterpene) cyclizes into the four-ring sterane structure.

N.question: In an α-helix, how many residues are there per turn?
N.explanation: The α-helix is right-handed, with 3.6 residues per turn and H-bonds between residue n and n+4.

N.question: Which amino acid is a strong α-helix breaker?
N.explanation: Proline's ring blocks rotation around the N–Cα bond and it lacks an N–H to donate an H-bond. Glycine also disfavours helices (too flexible).

N.question: In proteins, the peptide bond is mostly found in:
N.explanation: trans is more stable because it keeps the side chains apart. cis appears mainly before proline (about 5–10% of Pro).

N.question: Anfinsen's dogma states that:
options: Only enzymes have a native structure
The 3D structure is determined by the amino acid sequence
N.explanation: The native structure is the unique, stable, kinetically reachable free-energy minimum encoded by the sequence.

N.question: Which interaction stabilizing tertiary structure is covalent?
N.explanation: A disulfide bridge is a covalent bond between two cysteines; all the others are weak non-covalent interactions.

N.question: A holoprotein is made of:
options: A protein and a nucleic acid only
N.explanation: Conjugated protein: protein part (apoprotein) + non-protein part (prosthetic group), e.g. hemoglobin with heme.

N.question: Levinthal's paradox points out that:
options: A protein cannot find its native structure by randomly trying every conformation
All proteins have the same fold
N.explanation: Trying every conformation would take longer than the age of the universe, so folding must follow guided pathways.

N.question: With the 20 standard amino acids, how many different tripeptides are possible?
N.explanation: 20 choices at each of 3 positions: 20³ = 8,000 (dipeptides: 20² = 400).

N.question: A single collagen chain forms:
options: A left-handed helix with about 3.3 residues per turn
N.explanation: It is not an α-helix: each chain is left-handed; three of them wind into a right-handed superhelix.

N.question: Why must every third residue of collagen be glycine?
options: It is small enough to fit inside the triple helix
N.explanation: The centre of the triple helix has room only for glycine's single H side chain.

N.question: A permanent wave (curling hair) works by rearranging which bonds in α-keratin?
N.explanation: Reducing and then re-oxidizing the disulfide bridges fixes a new shape. Washing and drying only rearranges hydrogen bonds (temporary).

N.question: β-keratin, found in feathers, scales and claws, is mainly made of:
N.explanation: β-keratin (reptiles, birds) is rich in β-sheets; α-keratin (mammals: hair, nails, skin) is made of α-helices.

N.question: Collagen cross-links between chains start from:
N.explanation: Lysine is oxidized to allysine (an aldehyde), which reacts with Lys, OH-Lys or His to link chains together.

N.question: What does the hydroxylation of proline and lysine do in collagen?
options: Stabilizes the triple helix and enables cross-links and glycosylation
N.explanation: Hydroxyproline adds hydrogen bonds (also via water) that stabilize the triple helix; hydroxylysine allows glycosylation and cross-links.

N.question: Heating collagen produces:
N.explanation: Heat denatures the triple helix; on cooling, chains partly re-form helices randomly and trap water: a gel (gelatin).

N.question: In functional hemoglobin, heme iron is:
N.explanation: Only Fe²⁺ binds O₂. Oxidized Fe³⁺ (methemoglobin) cannot carry oxygen.

N.question: The fifth coordination site of the heme iron is occupied by:
N.explanation: Four sites bind the porphyrin nitrogens, the fifth the proximal His of the protein; the sixth binds O₂ (empty in deoxy forms).

N.question: The distal histidine lowers hemoglobin's affinity for CO because it:
options: Forces CO to bind at an angle
N.explanation: Free heme binds CO 25,000 times more than O₂; by forcing CO to bend, the distal His cuts that preference by about 100 times.

N.question: 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) in red blood cells:
options: Stabilizes the T state, lowering O₂ affinity
Stabilizes the R state, raising O₂ affinity
N.explanation: BPG holds hemoglobin in the T state so O₂ can be released in tissues. Fetal hemoglobin binds it poorly, so it has higher affinity.

N.question: Deoxyhemoglobin is in which conformational state?
N.explanation: The T state is held together by 8 salt bridges between subunits; O₂ binding breaks them and shifts towards R.

N.question: Hemoglobin is made of:
options: Two α and two β chains (two αβ dimers)
N.explanation: Tetramer α₂β₂: two identical αβ dimers, each chain similar to myoglobin.

N.question: In red blood cells, CO₂ is mostly converted to bicarbonate by:
N.explanation: Carbonic anhydrase speeds up CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → HCO₃⁻ + H⁺; HCO₃⁻ leaves the cell in exchange for Cl⁻ (chloride shift).

N.question: Compared with hemoglobin, myoglobin has:
N.explanation: Myoglobin is half-saturated at much lower O₂ pressure: it holds O₂ as a reserve, while hemoglobin must release it.

N.question: Enzymes change which property of a reaction?
N.explanation: Enzymes speed up a reaction by lowering the activation energy; equilibrium and ΔG stay the same.

N.question: An enzyme catalyzes a reaction because it binds most tightly:
N.explanation: Binding the transition state more than the substrate lowers its energy. A protein that only binds the substrate tightly does not catalyze.

N.question: An apoenzyme is:
options: The protein part alone, inactive without its cofactor
The active enzyme with its cofactor
N.explanation: Apoenzyme (protein only) is inactive; holoenzyme = apoenzyme + cofactor catalyzes.

N.question: In the induced-fit model:
options: The substrate is covalently modified first
The active site changes shape when the substrate binds
N.explanation: Lock-and-key assumes a rigid site; induced fit says both enzyme and substrate adjust when they bind.

N.question: Why do extreme pH values reduce enzyme activity?
options: They remove the active site's water
They change the charge of side chains and damage the 3D structure
N.explanation: At the optimal pH, acidic and basic residues have the right charge; away from it, the structure and the active site are altered.

N.question: An allosteric effector binds:
options: To a site other than the active site, changing the protein's shape
N.explanation: Allosteric = other site. Binding there changes conformation and so affinity or activity (2,3-BPG on hemoglobin is an example).

N.question: In Michaelis–Menten kinetics, at very high substrate concentration the rate:
N.explanation: When all active sites are busy (saturation), adding substrate no longer raises the rate: it approaches Vmax.
